transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-10-05
Start: 14:30 PDT
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Bennett (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Hawthorn Head of Platform), Liam Jones (SRE), Carlos Ruiz (InfoSec), Nina Chen (Product)

Summary: quick live demo of Console and API patterns for tenant keying and quota slicing, discuss dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs, security checklist and pilot next steps.

[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Sofia, I'm the AE for this account, and with me is Ethan our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Maya: Doing well, thanks. Excited to see the keying patterns you talked about.
[00:12] Ethan: Great, I put the agenda in the chat — quick architecture review, live Console walkthrough, then Optimize suggestions and pilot plan. We'll leave time for Qs.
[00:22] Liam: Cool. To set context — we run a multi-tenant API that spikes heavily during reports, so burst and fairshare are our main pain points. We also need strict audit logs and KMS integration.
[00:31] Carlos: From security: SOC 2 is fine, but we need to see encryption keys with HSM/KMS proof-of-concept. Also data residency concerns in eu-west.
[00:40] Ethan: Totally — we'll show the Private and Dedicated options and how KMS wiring looks. Just a note — some of the names in the console are short for things, sometimes the transcription will show KV as K-V cash, sorry for that.
[00:50] Sofia: Ok I'll hand it over to Ethan for the Console demo.
[00:52] Ethan: Alright sharing screen — first, the model catalog is here, then routing policies. For tenant keying we recommend an org->project key hierarchy. So you'd mint organization keys for Hawthorn-ingest, then project keys per product line. That lets you carve quotas at both levels.
[01:15] Maya: If we do org keys plus project keys, does billing break down per project automatically?
[01:20] Ethan: You can map project keys to billing centers via the Console tagging. In Hosted mode the billing line items are by project key; with Dedicated you'd set a committed capacity and we can map usage to org/project for internal chargebacks. There's a little nuance — if requests are routed across model variants the token counts still associate to the originating key.
[01:38] Liam: How does burst capacity work? Our reports can have 8k RPS bursts for 3–4 minutes.
[01:45] Ethan: Right, we have burst lanes. You can configure a baseline concurrency and then set a burst buffer. Also there's fairburst: it avoids a single tenant obliterating capacity by enforcing a per-key leaky bucket. In the Console you can set priority bands — e.g., gold/platinum lanes — and assign keys to them.
[02:05] Carlos: What about backpressure — will we see 429s or queueing? We need to avoid silent failures.
[02:12] Ethan: We expose clear status codes. 429 with a retry-after header for hard limits. For soft limits we can queue for up to X seconds based on SLOs. We also have sticky-routing so requests from the same key can prefer a warmed KV cache on a given shard — that reduces latency and cache thrash.
[02:32] Maya: Sticky what?
[02:34] Ethan: Sticky-routing — apologies, I mean sticky routing to keep the KV cache affinity. The transcription sometimes hyphenates words oddly.
[02:40] Nina: Can we control which keys are allowed to call tool functions? We have a subset of customers with tool-enabled prompts.
[02:46] Ethan: Yes, you can set per-key capabilities. In the Console we have 'capability policies' — function calling, streaming, embeddings. You can blacklist or whitelist.
[02:55] Sofia: Quick demo — switching to the project view. Here you can see per-route token breakdown, latency percentiles, and cost estimates. If you look at QPS over time you'll see sample spikes.
[03:10] [00:03:10] screen shows traffic graph (note: audio has some overlap)
[03:15] Ethan: Now I want to walk through a quota example. Let's say you want org-level committed capacity of 500k tokens/min, and per-project slices: prod=300k, reports=150k, dev=50k. You can set concurrency caps and burst allowances for each slice. The policy editor is declarative YAML but we have templates in the Console.
[03:40] Liam: If prod hits its slice, can it borrow from org pool automatically?
[03:44] Ethan: Yes, with a setting we call 'shared pool borrowing' — projects can borrow from unallocated org capacity subject to configurable caps and priority. Borrowing is accounted and you can create alerts for when a project borrows > x%.
[03:56] Maya: On SSO and RBAC — how granular is access control? We need role separation between infra and biz teams.
[04:02] Ethan: RBAC supports custom roles, and you can integrate with SAML/SSO. Admins can restrict who can create keys, who can modify quotas, and who can view billing.
[04:12] Carlos: And audit logs? Are they real-time? Can we ship to our SIEM?
[04:16] Ethan: Logs are exported to customer S3 or streaming to their SIEM via Kafka connector. We store immutable audit trails with key-level resolution and the console shows a timeline with actor IDs.
[04:28] Maya: For the Private deployment — how much work to wire KMS? I assume HSM-backed KMS is supported.
[04:33] Ethan: Yes, we support customer-managed KMS/HSM. For on-prem we offer a connector and we can do key wrapping. I'll attach our KMS runbook after the call.
[04:42] Carlos: Need to see a compliance diagram for encryption-at-rest and in-transit with key access models.
[04:48] Sofia: We'll send the security whitepaper and the network diagram.
[04:52] [00:04:52] quick silence, typing noises (shared links posted)
[05:00] Ethan: Now switching to Optimize tab — this suggests batching/quantization knobs based on your prompt size distribution. For example, if 70% of your calls are short completion requests, Optimize suggests small-seq optimized kernels and a batching window of 15ms.
[05:18] Maya: Does Optimize give cost delta estimates?
[05:21] Ethan: Yep — it shows projected per-1M token cost savings from batching and quantization and a risk score for potential quality regression. You can tie prompts to eval sets and get regression alerts.
[05:32] Nina: Could a change to quantization impact hallucination rates for our finance prompts?
[05:36] Ethan: It could; Optimize flags prompts with higher sensitivity and recommends running a focused eval set before rolling quantization wide.
[05:42] Liam: For the pilot we want to exercise report spikes and test warm cache hit rates. Can we run a targeted benchmark that simulates report-time mix?
[05:49] Ethan: Absolutely — we'll need your traffic histogram and a list of prompt templates. We'll run a 4-hour window with warm-up periods to replicate realistic KV cache priming.
[05:58] Maya: About invoices — we need per-team chargeback. If some teams go over quota and borrow, how is the billing charged?
[06:05] Ethan: You can enable per-project billing lines even under Dedicated. Borrowing is tagged and appears in billing breakdown, so internal chargebacks are possible.
[06:13] Carlos: Any restrictions around data retention for audit logs? We may need 7 years for certain logs.
[06:18] Ethan: We have retention policies configurable per account. Long-term archival to your S3 is supported for compliance.
[06:25] [00:06:25] small interruption (phone beep)
[06:30] Ethan: I'm going to show an example policy. Opening policy editor — here's a template named 'reporting-heavy'. It has leaky-bucket params: refill 1000 tokens/sec, burst 60s window, max-burst 60000 tokens. The policy also sets fallback routes to a cheaper rtx-2-small model variant if the high-capacity pool is saturated.
[06:52] Maya: If fallback occurs, can we keep requests but degrade quality gracefully? We need guaranteed minimum latency.
[06:58] Ethan: Yes, fallback can be configured with a 'quality floor' flag that refuses routing below a certain model capability. Otherwise it'll route to the fallback and include a header so your client knows the variant.
[07:08] Liam: For observability — can we get token-level traces? We want to trace an offending request through the runtime.
[07:13] Ethan: Yes — we have per-request traces that include model selection, routing decisions, and cache hits. The console allows you to search by key id and time range.
[07:22] Nina: Any SDK changes needed to switch keys on the client? We try to minimize rollout friction.
[07:26] Ethan: It's just the API key header. If you adopt project keys, you can rotate keys with zero-downtime by presenting the old and new key during a grace window while we ramp.
[07:36] Maya: Ok, can you show how to create a project key and assign quota?
[07:39] Ethan: Sure — new key -> attach to project -> quotas. Creating a key also gives you a configurable token-level policy, you can set caps per route and enable function-calling.
[07:50] [00:07:50] Ethan types and creates example key; slight audio lag noted
[08:00] Maria: sorry that was Maya not Maria; transcription misattributed earlier.
[08:05] Sofia: No worries — lots of names, auto-transcript sometimes flips them.
[08:09] Maya: For the pilot — timeline idea? We prefer a staged 4-week pilot: week1 smoke + security review, week2 scale tests, week3 performance tuning, week4 handover.
[08:20] Ethan: That works. Typical pilot includes dedicated capacity for the benchmark window or a hosted burst contract. We recommend dedicated for repeatable perf.
[08:30] Carlos: Is there an SLA during pilot? We need at least 99.5% uptime during test windows.
[08:36] Ethan: We can provide test-window SLA for the dedicated capacity. Production SLAs come with Reserved contracts.
[08:42] Sofia: I'll include SLA language in the pricing doc.
[08:46] Maya: Security review — we need network diagrams and pen test info.
[08:50] Sofia: We'll attach the security pack and SOC reports.
[08:53] [00:08:53] short pause
[09:00] Ethan: One more subtlety — request routing and cache affinity depend on the chosen keying scheme. If you use many ephemeral keys you get less cache hit rates. For reports, we suggest reusing project-level keys for report ingestion so KV cache warms.
[09:18] Liam: So ephemeral user keys for UI features, but stable project keys for background jobs. Makes sense.
[09:23] Nina: Any throttling behavior for embeddings vs completions?
[09:26] Ethan: You can set route-specific quotas. Embeddings can have separate throughput profiles. Optimize will also suggest quantization for embedding models where appropriate.
[09:34] Maya: Competitor question — we evaluated X provider but their quota model was too coarse. How do you compare?
[09:40] Sofia: We focus on fine-grained policy controls and cost/latency knobs — and a unified Console so ops doesn't need ad-hoc scripts.
[09:47] Carlos: Ok let's talk about pilot metrics. We need 95th p99 latency under 500ms for small-seq, and cache hit rate > 85% on warmed shards.
[09:57] Ethan: Noted. We'll design the benchmark to measure both token latency and cache hit rate.
[10:03] [00:10:03] brief cross-talk, someone typing
[10:10] Maya: About billing again — if team A borrows from team B and pushes over, we need automated alerts.
[10:16] Ethan: You can set alerting on borrow ratios; we'll send webhooks to your alerting system.
[10:22] Sofia: I'm going to summarize next steps at the end but first any more deep technical Qs?
[10:27] Carlos: One: can the audit logs include original prompt text or is it redacted by default?
[10:32] Ethan: Prompt storage is optional. We can store hashed or full prompts depending on your retention policy and compliance needs. Default is redacted with metadata.
[10:41] Maya: Can we get an example of the policy YAML you mentioned?
[10:44] Ethan: I'll paste one in the chat. (pastes policy) It has keys: resources, quotas, fallback routes, capabilities.
[10:52] [00:10:52] link posted: https://redwood.example/docs/policy-templates
[11:00] Nina: Are there any portability concerns if we later move from Dedicated to Private on-prem?
[11:06] Ethan: Minimal — our config is abstracted. The main work is network and KMS wiring. Model artifacts are the same.
[11:12] Liam: Ok last question — how do we handle emergency capacity increases?
[11:15] Sofia: We offer burst credits and emergency provisioning workflows; for dedicated customers we can pre-approve capacity bursts. We'll include options in the pricing sheet.
[11:25] Maya: Great. I think that's all from my side.
[11:28] Ethan: Awesome — I'll recap the pilot plan. Week1: security sign-off + smoke; Week2: scale tests with dedicated bench; Week3: tuning and Optimize changes; Week4: handover & runbook.
[11:41] Sofia: Thanks everyone — we'll send the pricing and security pack.
[11:44] Maya: Thanks, talk soon.

[46:30] End meeting

Notes: shared items in chat — policy template link, security pack placeholder, pricing sheet link (will be sent). Some transcript artifacts misattribute speakers (Maria/Maya) and mis-hyphenate K-V cache.
